Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: BlueHeron Payer Services x Redwood Inference — Procurement & contracting process
Date: 2026-02-06
Time: 3:00pm ET
Duration: 47 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Diego Fernandez (Redwood Inference, AE)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference, Solutions Engineering)
- Olga Petrov (Redwood Inference, GRC)
- Sofia Mendes (Redwood Inference, Commercial Counsel)
- Megan Park (BlueHeron, Procurement)
- Aaron Feldman (BlueHeron, Legal)
- Tanya Brooks (BlueHeron, Vendor Risk / GRC)
- Samir Shah (BlueHeron, Platform Engineering)

---
Summary (auto-generated)
BlueHeron walked Redwood through their vendor onboarding and contracting flow for an LLM inference vendor supporting regulated workloads. Discussion focused on MSA + order form structure, DPA/BAA requirements, SLA and support expectations, and what security evidence is needed to clear vendor risk. Timeline risks include BAA determination, security questionnaire turnaround, and aligning on Private/VPC scope vs Dedicated/hosted for the initial evaluation.

Topics
1) Contracting path: MSA → Order Form → DPA (+ possible BAA) → security addendum
2) SLA questions (uptime, credits, support response times) and what’s negotiable
3) Data handling + retention language; audit logs/export; subprocessors
4) Procurement timeline & gating items (insurance, pen test summary, vendor risk questionnaire)

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send latest MSA/order form and mark-up template
- BlueHeron to provide vendor risk questionnaire + required evidence
- Legal to confirm BAA requirement and whether evaluation can run pre-BAA
- Schedule follow-up once redlines are exchanged

---
Transcript

[00:00] Diego Fernandez: Cool. Alright, I think we’re on. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is pretty narrow—just walk through your procurement and legal steps, make sure we’re not surprised, and answer any SLA or contracting questions. Megan, Aaron, Tanya, Samir—appreciate it.

[00:18] Megan Park: Yep, thanks Diego. We’re trying to understand, like, best case and realistic case to get this through. Because the business is pushing hard.

[00:26] Diego Fernandez: Understood. Before we jump in, quick intros on our side. I’m Diego, account exec. Markus is solutions engineering, Olga is GRC, and Sofia is our commercial counsel.

[00:37] Aaron Feldman: Hi, Aaron, legal. I’ll be the person doing the redlines.

[00:41] Tanya Brooks: Tanya, vendor risk. I handle the questionnaires, SOC review, all that fun stuff.

[00:47] Samir Shah: Samir, platform. I’m the one who’ll get yelled at if we don’t have the right network diagram.

[00:52] (crosstalk)

[00:54] Diego Fernandez: Great. Megan—do you want to start with your process? Like, what are the gates.

[01:00] Megan Park: Sure. For a new vendor we typically do: intake request, vendor risk assessment, legal reviews the MSA and DPA, and then procurement negotiates commercial terms on the order form. If there’s PHI involved, we need a BAA. And then our security addendum is… it’s basically mandatory.

[01:22] Sofia Mendes: Helpful. When you say “security addendum,” is it your standard info-sec exhibit with specific controls, audit rights, incident notification, that kind of thing?

[01:31] Megan Park: Yes, exactly. It includes breach notice timelines and some… I think it has the right to pen test? Aaron can clarify.

[01:38] Aaron Feldman: It’s our standard. We don’t usually allow vendors to strike the audit language completely. We can sometimes narrow it to SOC reports, third-party audits, or reasonable cooperation.

[01:50] Sofia Mendes: That’s consistent with how we approach it. We generally can’t allow on-site audits into Redwood facilities, but we can support with SOC 2, written responses, and under NDA share a pen test summary.

[02:02] Tanya Brooks: Okay—so you do have SOC 2 Type II?

[02:05] Olga Petrov: Yes, SOC 2 Type II, current report. We can share under NDA. We also have a subprocessor list and change notification process.

[02:14] Tanya Brooks: Good. We’ll need that, plus insurance cert, vulnerability management overview, and incident response policy. And usually we ask for your data retention policy in writing.

[02:25] Diego Fernandez: Yep, that aligns with the addendum we already shared in the ABM pack. But we’ll follow your specific questionnaire.

[02:33] Samir Shah: Can I ask, before legal gets too deep—are we assuming Private deployment? Because the architecture choice changes a bunch of the security answers.

[02:41] Markus Klein: Great question. From the earlier calls, we heard you want VPC boundary, potentially your own KMS keys, and you don’t want prompts leaving a controlled network. That points to Redwood Private in VPC. But we’re also open to starting with Dedicated if that helps accelerate.

[02:58] Samir Shah: Right, but procurement wants timelines, so…

[03:02] Diego Fernandez: Yeah. We can talk through both. The contracting path is similar, but BAA and data flow language get tighter if you’re doing PHI with hosted.

[03:14] Aaron Feldman: That’s the key point. If it’s PHI, it’s BAA and we’re strict about the DPA. If it’s “no PHI in the evaluation,” we might be able to do an evaluation agreement first.

[03:26] Megan Park: Exactly. We can do a short-form eval with limited data and then do full MSA/BAA for production.

[03:33] Diego Fernandez: That’s helpful. Can we confirm: for the first 2–3 week POC, would you be willing to run synthetic or de-identified data? Or do you expect to run real member data.

[03:45] Samir Shah: We can do de-identified for the first pass. But the real value is in prior auth notes, which is… not trivial to de-identify.

[03:56] Tanya Brooks: Even de-identified, we still treat it as regulated. But BAA requirement is typically tied to PHI.

[04:03] Olga Petrov: Understood. We can support a “no PHI” evaluation and still provide the same security evidence. For Private in your VPC, prompts and outputs stay in your network boundary, and we can configure retention controls per the deployment.

[04:20] Aaron Feldman: I want to be precise here. When you say “stay in our boundary,” you mean the inference runtime is deployed in our VPC and the traffic doesn’t traverse public internet?

[04:30] Markus Klein: Correct. Private deployment can be in your VPC with private connectivity. Control plane components are separate; we can walk the shared responsibility model. But the inference request path can be private.

[04:44] Samir Shah: And logs? Like request logs, token logs. Where do those go.

[04:50] Markus Klein: For Private, we can configure what gets logged. We have audit logs for admin actions and operational logs. For request/response content logging, the default posture for regulated is minimal—metadata, not payloads—unless you explicitly enable more. And we can export logs to your SIEM.

[05:10] Tanya Brooks: That’s the kind of statement I need in a questionnaire: “do you store prompts and outputs.”

[05:15] Olga Petrov: We can provide approved language. The exact answer depends on the deployment mode and configuration. For Private, the customer controls the environment and can decide retention settings for certain logs.

[05:27] Diego Fernandez: We’ll send the approved retention and residency statement we use for regulated workloads.

[05:34] Megan Park: Okay. Switching gears—SLA. If we’re paying for dedicated or private, what SLA do you offer? Uptime, response times, credits.

[05:45] Diego Fernandez: Standard enterprise SLA is 99.9% for the service during the term, with service credits if we miss it. For Dedicated and Private, we scope it in the order form and SLA exhibit. Latency SLA tends to be more like SLOs—depends on model and your request patterns.

[06:03] Aaron Feldman: In our vendor addendum we have a 99.9 uptime expectation too, but we also have breach notice within 24 hours.

[06:12] Sofia Mendes: We typically commit to notification without undue delay, and a specific window for confirmed security incidents. 24 hours for initial notice can be tough depending on investigation, but we can look at it.

[06:26] (crosstalk)

[06:27] Tanya Brooks: We do require 72 hours in some places and 24 in others. I’ll send the exact clause.

[06:33] Sofia Mendes: Great. We’ll review it.

[06:36] Megan Park: Support coverage—do you have 24/7?

[06:39] Diego Fernandez: For Private and Dedicated, we have premium support tiers, including 24/7 for severity 1. We can map your expectations to the right tier. Markus, do you want to add anything.

[06:53] Markus Klein: The biggest thing is escalation path during a POC. We usually set a Slack or email channel, agree on response times, and for production the support SLA governs.

[07:03] Samir Shah: That matters because if we do a POC and it flakes out, we’ll lose internal support.

[07:08] Diego Fernandez: Totally. That’s why we like to document success criteria and also—if you want—set up a weekly check-in.

[07:16] Megan Park: Commercially, we’re expecting an order form with pricing, term, and what exactly we’re buying—Dedicated vs Private license.

[07:25] Diego Fernandez: Right. Our structure usually: MSA + order form. For Private there’s platform fee + support, and for Dedicated it’s reserved capacity with a commit. For the POC we can do a limited evaluation order form or a pilot addendum, within our guardrails.

[07:44] Aaron Feldman: Okay. Data protection. Do you have a DPA template, or are you taking ours.

[07:50] Sofia Mendes: We can start from either. Many customers prefer their DPA. The biggest points we look at are: definitions of personal data, processor/controller roles, subprocessors, security measures, and cross-border transfer language.

[08:06] Aaron Feldman: We’re US-based but we do reference GDPR because some members are… well, long story. But mostly we just want standard SCC language if needed.

[08:17] Olga Petrov: We have SCC addendum language available. Again, under NDA we can share our standard.

[08:23] Tanya Brooks: Also we need to know where data is processed. Residency.

[08:28] Markus Klein: For Private in your VPC, processing is in your chosen cloud region/account. For Hosted API, it’s in Redwood-managed cloud regions. That’s why the deployment mode decision is key.

[08:44] Samir Shah: So if we pick Private, procurement timeline might be longer because of the install? Or shorter because it avoids BAA? Not sure.

[08:54] Diego Fernandez: It can go either way. Private sometimes has more technical work upfront—networking, IAM, logging—but it can simplify some data handling concerns. BAA depends on whether you’re sending PHI to a business associate. If the runtime is in your VPC and we’re not accessing PHI, there’s an argument it’s different, but that’s a legal call.

[09:15] Aaron Feldman: Yeah. We’ll decide. I’m not going to commit on the call.

[09:19] Diego Fernandez: Totally fair.

[09:22] Megan Park: Timeline-wise, best case, if we get redlines back quickly, legal review is 1–2 weeks. Vendor risk is often the longest; Tanya, what do you see.

[09:31] Tanya Brooks: If the vendor is responsive, and the SOC report doesn’t have big exceptions, we can do it in 10 business days. But if we need clarifications, or if there’s a BAA negotiation, it can stretch to 3–4 weeks.

[09:46] Sofia Mendes: And are there fixed committee meetings? Like a weekly risk council.

[09:51] Tanya Brooks: Yes, Thursdays. If you miss the Thursday packet, it pushes a week.

[09:57] Diego Fernandez: That’s a good timeline risk to flag.

[10:00] (pause)

[10:02] Diego Fernandez: Let’s talk SLA specifics. What are you expecting for uptime and remedies.

[10:08] Megan Park: We prefer 99.9. Credits should be meaningful, but not crazy. We also care about response times: Sev 1 within 30 minutes.

[10:17] Diego Fernandez: We can align. For Sev 1, we generally target fast response under premium support.

[10:24] Aaron Feldman: Also limitation of liability. Our standard is 2x fees, with carve-outs for confidentiality and data security.

[10:33] Sofia Mendes: We commonly see that. Our standard has caps and standard carve-outs; we can review against your terms.

[10:43] Aaron Feldman: And indemnities. Specifically, IP indemnity for the platform and the models.

[10:50] Diego Fernandez: On models, we’re typically serving open models and we can talk through the licensing posture. Sofia can speak to contract language.

[10:58] Sofia Mendes: We generally provide IP indemnity for our technology. Model indemnity varies based on the model provider and licensing; we’ll be transparent in the order form about the model catalog and any limitations.

[11:11] Samir Shah: We’re also evaluating Bedrock and Azure OpenAI. They have very standard terms. That’s why procurement is asking “why are you different.”

[11:22] Diego Fernandez: Makes sense. The reason teams pick us in regulated workloads is the deployment flexibility—Hosted to Dedicated to Private—plus performance/cost controls. But we’ll keep this call on procurement.

[11:34] Megan Park: Okay. Security addendum: we require encryption at rest and in transit. Any exceptions.

[11:40] Olga Petrov: No exceptions. TLS in transit. At rest encryption depends on the storage component; for Private you use your cloud native encryption; for Hosted we use cloud provider managed encryption and can integrate with KMS for key management in certain modes.

[11:58] Tanya Brooks: We require customer-managed keys for PHI.

[12:02] Markus Klein: In Private, you can use your own KMS keys because it’s in your account. In Hosted, we can discuss key management options, but the straightforward answer is Private gives you maximum control.

[12:18] Samir Shah: That’s why we’ve been pushing Private.

[12:20] Megan Park: But Private usually means longer procurement because we treat it like software, not a SaaS.

[12:26] Diego Fernandez: Understood. We can structure it cleanly: a software license + support, with the deployment architecture documented.

[12:35] Aaron Feldman: BAA—do you have a template.

[12:38] Sofia Mendes: Yes. We can provide our standard BAA and we can also review yours. Many healthcare customers prefer their own.

[12:47] Tanya Brooks: If you can send it, I’ll add it to the package for next Thursday.

[12:52] Diego Fernandez: We can do that.

[12:55] Megan Park: One more thing: subcontractors. We need your list, and we need notification if it changes.

[13:02] Olga Petrov: We have a published list and a process for advance notice of material changes.

[13:08] Tanya Brooks: “Advance notice” meaning 30 days.

[13:11] Olga Petrov: Typically 30 days, yes.

[13:14] Aaron Feldman: Audit logs. We want audit logs available for at least one year.

[13:19] Markus Klein: For Private, logs retention depends on your logging stack; we can stream to your SIEM and you set retention. For Hosted, audit logs are available and retention varies by plan; we can align with your needs.

[13:34] Samir Shah: And export format—like Splunk HEC, S3, whatever.

[13:38] Markus Klein: We support common export patterns. For Private, easiest is shipping to your existing pipeline. I’ll send a one-pager with options.

[13:49] Diego Fernandez: Great.

[13:51] Megan Park: Okay, can we enumerate the actual contracting steps so I can update my tracker.

[13:57] Diego Fernandez: Yes. From Redwood side, we’ll send: MSA, order form, DPA, and if needed BAA. You’ll do initial redlines. We’ll respond. Parallel, Tanya runs vendor risk questionnaire and collects evidence.

[14:13] Megan Park: And the security addendum, you’ll sign ours.

[14:16] Sofia Mendes: We’ll review and propose edits where necessary.

[14:20] Megan Park: Once legal agrees, procurement finalizes pricing and signature. Then we can issue a PO.

[14:27] Diego Fernandez: Perfect.

[14:28] (short silence)

[14:30] Aaron Feldman: I want to ask about incident response. Your standard says something like “prompt notice.” Our addendum requires specific: initial notice within 24 hours, updates every 48 hours until closure.

[14:44] Sofia Mendes: We can usually agree to a structured update cadence once we’ve confirmed an incident affecting your data. The 24-hour initial notice—let’s look at the exact language. Sometimes we can do “within 48 hours of confirmation” or “without undue delay, not to exceed X.”

[15:03] Tanya Brooks: We can be flexible if there’s a clear commitment.

[15:06] Aaron Feldman: Another clause is audit rights: we require right to audit once per year. Vendors hate it.

[15:14] Sofia Mendes: Yeah. We typically satisfy that through providing SOC 2 report and responding to reasonable questionnaires. Direct audits can be limited to those artifacts unless a regulator requires something else.

[15:28] Aaron Feldman: Understood. We might be able to accept that with a carve-out.

[15:33] Diego Fernandez: On timeline—what’s the biggest risk to miss your internal deadline.

[15:38] Megan Park: Two things. One, if we decide we need a BAA and it gets negotiated back and forth. Two, if vendor risk needs additional evidence and it misses the Thursday meeting.

[15:52] Diego Fernandez: Got it. Our mitigation: we’ll send docs immediately, and we’ll assign Olga as the point person for questionnaire responses.

[16:02] Olga Petrov: Yep. We can also do a 30-minute vendor risk walkthrough if you want—sometimes it’s faster than email.

[16:09] Tanya Brooks: That helps.

[16:11] Samir Shah: For technical—do we need a statement of work for the install.

[16:17] Diego Fernandez: Usually no formal SOW for standard Private in VPC, but if you want professional services, we can add it. Markus can scope.

[16:27] Markus Klein: Most of the work is configuration and validation: networking (VPC peering or private link), DNS/TLS, IAM roles, logging export. We can document responsibilities.

[16:40] Samir Shah: Good.

[16:41] Megan Park: And if we start with Dedicated while Private is being set up, is that feasible contractually.

[16:49] Diego Fernandez: Potentially. But we’d want to avoid two separate negotiations. We can write an order form that includes an evaluation phase and then conversion to Private.

[17:02] Aaron Feldman: Like a ramp schedule.

[17:04] Diego Fernandez: Exactly.

[17:06] Megan Park: Okay.

[17:08] (Fireflies note: audio overlap)

[17:10] Tanya Brooks: One more security thing: do you do background checks for employees.

[17:14] Olga Petrov: Yes, for employees with access to production systems. We can provide policy description.

[17:20] Tanya Brooks: And do you have a bug bounty.

[17:22] Olga Petrov: We have a vulnerability disclosure program; I’ll confirm whether it’s a formal bounty. We can share details.

[17:31] Aaron Feldman: Data deletion. We need right to request deletion at termination.

[17:36] Sofia Mendes: That’s standard. For Private in your VPC, you can delete directly. For any Redwood-held data (like account metadata), we have retention periods and deletion process. We’ll align it in the DPA.

[17:53] Samir Shah: Wait, account metadata—like logs of admin actions.

[17:56] Markus Klein: Exactly—audit logs, operational metrics, not your payload content by default.

[18:03] Diego Fernandez: Great.

[18:05] Megan Park: I think that covers procurement. What do you need from us.

[18:10] Diego Fernandez: A few things. (1) Your security addendum and your DPA/BAA templates, if you prefer those. (2) Your vendor risk questionnaire checklist so Olga can start. (3) Confirmation on whether the POC will be “no PHI.”

[18:27] Aaron Feldman: I’ll send the templates today.

[18:29] Tanya Brooks: I’ll send the questionnaire—likely Monday. We’re updating it.

[18:33] Megan Park: And I’ll put a hold for next week follow-up.

[18:36] Diego Fernandez: Perfect.

[18:38] (pause)

[18:40] Markus Klein: Samir, quick check: for Private in VPC, do you have a preference: AWS vs Azure.

[18:47] Samir Shah: We’re mostly AWS. We can do VPC peering. PrivateLink is better but it depends.

[18:53] Markus Klein: Got it. We’ll send our assumptions and you can tell us what’s feasible.

[19:00] Diego Fernandez: Before we wrap, any last SLA questions.

[19:04] Megan Park: Service credits. If uptime is below 99.9, what’s the credit schedule.

[19:10] Diego Fernandez: It’s tiered. We can share the exhibit. It’s typically a percentage of the monthly fees.

[19:18] Aaron Feldman: And do you exclude maintenance.

[19:21] Diego Fernandez: Planned maintenance is excluded if we notify; emergency maintenance is handled differently.

[19:28] Aaron Feldman: Okay.

[19:30] Sofia Mendes: Also, any special procurement requirements—like required payment terms.

[19:35] Megan Park: Net 60 is preferred. Net 45 sometimes.

[19:38] Diego Fernandez: We’ll see what we can do.

[19:41] Diego Fernandez: Alright. Thanks everyone. We’ll send the doc package today/tomorrow, and then we’ll schedule follow-up once Aaron has initial redlines.

[19:51] Megan Park: Sounds good.

[19:53] Tanya Brooks: Thanks.

[19:54] Aaron Feldman: Thanks.

[19:55] Samir Shah: Thanks.

[19:57] Meeting ended.
